AURANGZEB. J.- Through this constitutional petition under Article 199 of the constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973, the petitioner has challenged Office Order No' 598-604lDC IAE/F-8 dated 29.1O.2025, whereby Registry No. 591, Bahi No' 01, Jild No' 626' dated 30.03.2023, executed in her favour, was cancelled in purported exercise of powers under section 6s(2) of the Registration Act, 1908 (hereinafter referred to as "the Act"), with a consequential direction to the Sub- Registrar, Bannu, to make corresponding corrections in the revenue record. She has also called in question four fact-finding inquiries and letterNo.LR-lV/PF/TajMaliKhan/8325-28dated15.10.2025,issuedby the Assistant Director Land Records, besides seeking departmental and legal action against Respondent No. 6, the Deputy Commissioner, Bannu' 2. The facts, in brief, are that the petitioner is tJ:e widow of late professor subhan Nazir, who, during his lifetime, executed the aforesaid registered instrument in her favour in lieu of her dower, transferring land measuring 127 Kanals and 11 Marlas situated, in different mouzas of District Bannu. The instrument was registered in the office of the Sub- Registrar, Bannu, in the presence of two marginal witnesses, namely Rahmat Qabil and Jamshid Khan, sons of Mameez Khan, stated to be real nephews of t}re executant. The executant died on 24.L2.2O23, approximately nine months after registration. According to the petitioner, Respondent No. 15, Atlas Khan, brother of the deceased, thereafter pressurized her to transfer the property in his favour. Upon her refusal, he approached different forums and lodged complaints against the transaction, including before the Registrar and the Anti-Corruption Establishment. The inquiry conducted by the Anti-Cornrption Establishment was filed, whereas the proceedings before the learned Justice of Peace were set aside by this Court in W.P. No. 371-8 of 2025, decided on 07 .1O.2O25, for want of lawful jurisdiction.

3. Subsequently, Respondent No. 15 approached the Senior Member, Board of Revenue, whereupon the Director Land Records (Inspector General of Registration), through the Assistant Director Land Records, issued letter No. LRJV/PF/Taj Mali l(hanl8325-28 dated L5.1O.2O25, directing further action. Different revenue authorities conducted four fact-finding inquiries and, on the basis of their reports and recommendations, Office Order No. 598-604lDC|AE/F-8 dated 29.1O.2O25 was issued, whereby the registered instrument was ordered to be cancelled under Section 68(2) of the Act and the Sub-Registrar was directed to make corresponding corrections in the revenue record. The petitioner maintains that she was not associated with most of the inquiries and was not afforded an effective opportunity of hearing before the impugned order was passed.

4. karned counsel for the petitioner contended that Section 68(21 ot the Act confers only supenrisory and corrective powers upon the Registrar and does not authorize cancellation of an instrument after registration on allegations of fraud, misrepresentation or want of title. It was further argued that the impugned order was issued by the Additional Deputy Commissioner on behalf of the Deputy Commissioner without establishing his lawful competence to exercise the powers of the Registrar. Conversely, learned counsel for the respondents supported the impugned action on the basis of the fact-finding reports and the alleged irregularities surrounding the transaction.
5. We have heard learned counsel for the parties and examined the available record, including the additional documents placed on record through C.M. No. 356-B of 2026.

6. The principal question requiring determination is not merely whether the allegations levelled against the registered transaction warranted an inquiry, but whether the Registration Act, 1908, empowers the Registrar or any other registering authority to cancel an instrument after its registration has been completed. This question necessarily involves examination of the nature and extent of supervisory jurisdiction under Section 68(2) of the Act; the distinction between rectilication of an error concerning a registration book or office and cancellation of the registered instrument itself; the scope of the registering officer's inquiry under Sections 34 and 35, read with Sections 36 to 39 and 58 to 61; the effect of the refusal and remedial mechanism provided under Sections 71 to 77; and the relevance of Section 71(l-A), inserted through the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Registration (Amendment) Act, 2014. It also requires consideration of Rules 2 and 135 of the West Pakistan Registration Rules, 1929, which had already been adopted and made applicable in the Province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa by the Provincial Government before the subsequent amendments notified on O5.1O.2O26. The subsequent notification and its effect upon the exisdng regulatory framework also require consideration. In addition, the competence of the officer who issued the impugned order, the legal effect of the four fact-finding inquiries, the protection contemplated under Section 87 of the Act and the requirement of an opportunity of hearing must be examined. Ultimately, the question is whether allegations of fraud, impersonation, want of title or infringement of third-party rights can be determined through administrative proceedings under the Act, or whether such controversies require adjudication by a competent civil court under Section 39 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877 , read with Section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

7. The Registration Act, 1908, provides a statutory framework governing presentation, admission, registration and preservation of documents. Sections 6 and 7 deal with the appointment of registering officers and establishment of their offices, whereas Sections l0 and 11 regulate arrangements during the absence of a Registrar or a temporary vacErncy in his office. Sections 34 and 35 prescribe the inquiry to be conducted before registration, principally concerning the appearance and identity of the executant, his authority where applicable, and admission or denial ofexecution. Sections 36 to 39 provide tJre procedural machinery for securing the appearance of executants and witnesses. These provisions regulate the process of registration and do not constitute the registering officer as a civil court competent to adjudicate disputed questions of ownership, fraud or the substantive validity of a transaction.

8. Sections 34 and 35 are particularly relevant to the extent of the registering oflicer's jurisdiction. Under Section 34, the registering officer is required to inquire whether the document was executed by the persons by whom it purports to have been executed, satisfy himself as to the identity of the persons appearing before him and, where a representative, assign or agent appears, ascertain his authority. Section 35 provides the procedure where execution is admitted or denied. The inquiry is directed towards compliance with the statutory requirements for registration. It does not authorize a registering officer to conduct a civil trial concerning ownership of the property or to adjudicate upon competing claims of persons who are not parties to the transaction.

9. Sections 58 to 61 deal with endorsements, signatures, certificates and completion of registration. In particular, Section 60 provides for endorsement of the certificate of registration, while Section 61 deals with copying the endorsements and certificate into the relevant register-book and completion of registration. The certificate of registration is admissible to prove that the document has been duly registered in the manner provided by law and that the facts mentioned in the endorsements have occurred as stated therein. Section 61 expressly provides that registration shall be deemed complete upon compliance with the prescribed requirements. Registration does not, by itself, conclusively establish title or render an instrument immune from judicial challenge. Nevertheless, once the statutory process has been completed, the instrument cannot be administratively annulled in the absence of an express enabling provision.
10. Since the impugned order purports to have been passed under Section 68(2) ofthe Act, it is appropriate to reproduce the provision in its original form:

"68. Power of Registrar to superintend and control Sub- Registrars.-(1) Every Sub-Registrar shall perform the duties of his office under the superintendence and control of the Registrar in whose district the office of such Sub-Registrar is situate.

(2) Every Registrar shall have authority to issue (whether on complaint or otherwise) any order consistent with this Act which he considers necessary in respect of any act or omission of any Sub-Registrar subordinate to him or in respect of the rectification of any error regarding the book or the office in which any document has been registered."

11. A plain reading of the above provision demonstrates that the powers conferred upon the Registrar are supervisory and corrective in character. Subsection (1) places the Sub-Registrar under the superintendence and control of the RegisEar, whereas subsection (2) authorizes the Registrar to issue orders consistent with the Act in respect of any act or omission of a subordinate sub-Registrar or for rectification of an error concerning the book or office in which a document has been registered' The expression "any order consistent with this Act" cannot be interpreted as conferring unrestricted jurisdiction to annul an instrument or determine competing claims of ownership. The power to rectify an error in a registration book or office is legally distinct from the power to cancel the instrument itself. The latter involves determination of substantive civil rights, which cannot be undertaken by an administrative authority in the absence of express statutory authorization.

12. Section 69 confers general superintendence over registration offices upon the Inspector General of Registration and empowers him to frame rules consistent with the Act, subject to the prescribed statutory requirements. Section 7o concerns remission of fines imposed under sections 25 and 34 and is liscal and procedural in nature. Neither provision authorzes cancellation of an already registered instrument. Likewise, sections 7l to 77 prescribe the procedure for refusal of registration and the remedies available against such refusal. These provisions operate at the stage of registration and do not provide a correspondingpowertocanceladocumentafterregistrationhasbeen completed. The legislature has thus provided a specific mechanism for refusal of registration and remedies against such refusal' but has not vested the Registrar with a general power to cancel a completed registration on allegations of fraud or want of title' 13. The Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Registration (Amendment) Act' 2Ol4' being Act No. XXXIII of 2014, published in the Extraordinary Gazette dated 20.11.2014, inserted subsection (1-A) in Section 71 of the Act' requiring the Sub-Registrar to refuse registration where the person concerned does not hold valid title or rights in the immovable property on the date the deed of alienation is presented for attestation. The amendment is relevant to the scrutiny required at the initial stage of registration. It does not confer upon the Registrar a corresponding power to cancel a document after registration. The distinction between refusal at the registration stage and cancellation after completion of registration must be maintained. The amendment cannot be read as supplying a power which the legislature has not expressly conferred.

14. The West Pakistan Registration Rules, 1929, framed under the Registration Act, 1908, also require consideration. It is pertinent to clari$r that the said Rules had already been adopted and made applicable by the Provincial Government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa before the issuance of the subsequent notification dated 05. 10.2026. Their application in the Province, therefore, does not originate from the said notification. The notification issued by the Board of Revenue, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, bearing No. LR-MII/Registration-Rules Arrrendmer.t/24117 dated O5.LO.2O26, and published in the Extraordinar5r Government Gezette dated 15.10.2026, constitutes a subsequent amendment to the existing Ru1es. It was issued by the Inspector General of Registration, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, in exercise of powers conferred by Section 69 of the Act, with the approval of the Provincial Government. Through the said notification, certain terminological and substantive amendments were introduced, including substitution of the word "Punjab" with "Khyber Pakhtunkhwa" wherever occurring and substitution of the expressions "Government of the Punjab" and "Provincial Government of the Punjab" with the word "Government". The existing Rule 1 was renumbered as Rule 1-A, and a new Rule 1 was inserted, providing that the Rules shall be called the West Pakistan Registration Rules, 1929, and shall come into force at once. The notification must, therefore, be understood in its proper context as a subsequent amendment of the already adopted Rules and not as the original instrument through which the Rules were first made applicable in the Province.

15. Rule 2 of the West Pakistan Registration Rules, 1929, deals with the classes and designation of registering officers and the administrative arrangement governing registration offices. Its application in the Province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa is to be understood in the light of the earlier provincial adoption of the Rules and the subsequent amendments made thereto. The designation of an officer as Additional Deputy Commissioner, by itself, does not establish that he has acquired tJle statutory powers of the Registrar. Such authority must be traceable to the Act, the applicable Rules or a lawful appointment or authorization made thereunder' The relevant statutory provisions governing the appointment and exercise of powers by a Registrar must, therefore, be strictly observed' 16. Rule 135 of the West Pakistan Registration Rules, 1929, is particularly relevant to the controversy. It provides, in substance, that registering officers are not concerned with the substantive validity of documents presented for registration and should not refuse registration merely because the executant may be dealing with property not belonging tohim,theinstrumentmayinfringetherightsofthirdparties,orthe transaction may be fraudulent or opposed to public policy' Such matters are left for determination by competent courts of law' The rule further requires the registering officer, where a document is properly presented by a competent person, at the proper offrce and within the prescribed time, and the identity of the executant and his admission of execution are established, to proceed with registration without adjudicating upon the possiblelegaleffectsofthetransaction.Itissignificantthatthe subsequent notification dated 05.10'2026 does not repeal or substitute Rule 135. The existing rule continues to operate as part of the regulatory framework, subject to the applicable amendments and the overriding provisions of the Registration Act, 1908. The principle embodied in Rule 135 must, therefore, be read harmoniously with Section 71(1-A)' inserted through the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Registration (Amendment) Act' 2014' which specifically requires scrutiny of title at the initial stage of registration. Neither Rule 135 nor the said amendment confers upon a registering authority the power to cancel an instrument after registration has been comPleted.

has also introduced and digitization of The subsequent notification dated provisions concerning electronic 05.10.2026 registration registration records. These include the insertion of an explanation in Rule 41 concerning electronic records;

amendment of Rule 42 tegatdirrg preservation of electronic records through secure servers and accesscontrolled systems; provision for electronic inspection under Rule 53; recognition of certified electronic records and digitally signed extracts under Rule 54; maintenance of statutory registers in electronic form under Rule 57; and, insertion of Rule 58-A concerning the legal status of electronic records. Further amendments have been made to Rules 60 and 61 concerning electronic closure certificates and system-generated serial numbers, dates and times, while Rule 71 now recognizes digitally generated and authenticated orders of refusal of registration, and Rule 108 permits proceedings of a commission to be recorded and transmitted electronically. These amendments modernize the existing registration framework and recognize electronic records and processes within the statutory system. However, none of these amendments confers upon the Registrar or any other registering officer an independent power to cancel an instrument after completion of its registration. Moreover, the subsequent amendments cannot retrospectively be invoked to determine the legality of the impugned order dated 29 .LO.2O25. The scope of Section 68(2) of the Act, therefore, remains governed by its express statutory language and cannot be enlarged through amendments dealing with electronic registration and preservation of records.

17. The distinction between an erTor in the registration process and an alleged defect in the underlying transaction is fundamental. If a document is registered in an unauthorized oflice or an entry is incorrectly made in a registration book, the competent authority may exercise such corrective powers as are expressly conferred by the Act. However, where the complaint is that the executant had no title, the transaction was fraudulent, the instrument was procured through misrepresentation or the rights of a third party have been infringed, the controversy concerns the substantive validity of the transaction. Such questions cannot be determined by invoking the administrative power of superintendence under Section 68(2).
1g. The question of administrative cancellation of a registered instrument has received judicial consideration by this court. In C.R. No.

355-P of 2017, decided on C,3.06.2024, this Court examined the legality of an order dated 23.O6.2O10 passed by the DDOR/Sub-Registrar cancelling a registered instrument. The cancellation was held to be illegal on the ground that the Registration Act, 1908, does not confer upon the registering authority the power to recall or cancel a document after registration has been completed' The Court also considered the principles discussed in Park View Enterprises and Satya Pal Anand, particularly the distinction between the statutory function of registration and adjudication of allegations of fraud or impersonation. The principle laid down therein is directly relevant to the present controversy' The registering authority cannot assume jurisdiction to cancel a completed registration merely because a complaint raises allegations concerning the genuineness or legal effect of the transaction.

lg. The same principle finds support from Amlr Jq.ma and others o. Ma l-Hao othc 12011 SCUR I O231. wherein the Honourable Supreme court dealt with the cancellation of a registered instrument in constitutional proceedings and emphasized the need for adjudication of disputed questions of title and fraud through appropriate civil proceedings. The decision reinforces the proposition that disputed questions concerning the validity of a registered instrument cannot ordinarily be determined by exercising writ jurisdiction or administrative powersinsubstitutionofaciviltrial.Theremedyforcancellationofavoid or voidable instrument is provided under Section 39 of ttle Specific Relief Act, 1877.

20. lnHu ln ll Shd v. Sardor A Sha,hINRT 33 Lahote 78 6t. the limited nature of the Registrar's powers under Section 68 was recogrrized, and it was held that the provision does not authorize cancellation of a registered document' The same principle was followed in luh o18 YI,R 77 wherein it was reiterated that the Registrar cannot assume the jurisdiction of a civil court to cancel a registered instrument on allegations concerning its validity' 21. Reference may also be made to Mohawsd lbrorhlm ttvouoh I v.

I I'U At In that case' the Sindh High Court examined the legality of executive action affecting rights founded upon registered instruments, namely assignment and lease deeds. The court held that cancellation of a registered document could take place through a declaration of a competent court and not by means of an executive order. Although the factual setting of that case concerned industrial plots and administrative action by a public authority' the l0 principle is relevant to the present controversy: an executive authority cannot, in the absence of statutory power, extinguish rights claimed under a registered instrument by issuing an administrative cancellation order. The said judgment, therefore, lends support to tJle distinction between executive action and judicial cancellation of a registered instrument.

22. Section 39 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877, provides a remedy to a person against whom a written instrument is void or voidable and who has reasonable apprehension that its continued existence may cause serious injury. Such person may institute a suit for cancellation before the competent civil court. The provision reads:

When cancellatlon may be ordered.- Any person against whom a written instrument is void or voidable, who has reasonable apprehension that such instrument, if left outstanding, may cause him serious injury, may sue to have it adjudged void or voidable; and the Court may, in its discretion, so adjudge it and order it to be delivered up and cancelled."

The language of the provision makes it clear that the person seeking cancellation must approach the Court and establish the grounds justifying such relief. Section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, recognizes the jurisdiction of civil courts to try all suits of a civil nature unless their jurisdiction is expressly or impliedly barred. Whether the deceased voluntarily executed the instrument, whether he possessed lawful title to the property, whether the transaction was genuinely made in lieu of dower, or whether fraud, impersonation or misrepresentation was involved, are questions requiring evidence and adjudication by the competent civil court.

23. The legal distinction must, therefore, be kept clear. The setting aside of the administrative order cancelling the registration does not amount to a judicial declaration that the underlying instrument is valid, nor does it establish the petitioner's title to the property. Equally, the fact that a document has been registered does not prevent a person having a lawful cause of action from challenging it before a competent civil court. The registration record and the substantive validity of the transaction are l1 separate matters. The former is governed by the Registration Act, whereas ttre latter, where disputed, is to be determined through appropriate civil proceedings.

24. In the present case, Respondent No. 15 disputes the genuineness and legal effect of the transaction and asserts rights adverse to those claimed by the petitioner. Such controversy cannot be conclusively determined through departmental inquiries or administrative correspondence. Even if the inquiries disclosed circumstances casting doubt upon the transaction, the appropriate course was to place the relevant material before the competent forum for proceedings in accordance with law. Neither the inquiries nor letter dated 15.1O.2025 could enlarge the jurisdiction of the Registrar or furnish independent authority for cancellation of the registered instrument' 25. The impugned order suffers from an additional defect concerning the competence of the officer who issued it. The record reveals that it was signed by the Assistant Commissioner on behalf of the Deputy Commissioner. No lawful appointment, notification or statutory authorization empowering the Assistant Commissioner to exercise the powers of the Registrar under Section 68 has been produced' Section 10 of the Act provides for appointment of a person to act as Registrar during an absence otherwise than on duty within the district or a temporary vacancy, whereas Section 11 deals with the Registrar's absence on duty withinhisdistrictandexpresslyexcludesthepowersunderSections68 and,T2fromthedutieswhichmaybeassigrredt]rereunder.Themerefact thattheorderwasissuedonbehalfoftheDeputyCommissionerdoesnot establish the requisite statutory competence' 26. we have also considered Section 87 of the Act, which provides t].at an act done in good faith pursuant to the Act shall not be deemed invalid merely by reason of a defect in the appointment or procedure of a registering officer. The protection contemplated by this provision must' however, be distinguished from the assumption of a substantive jurisdiction which the Act does not confer' Section 87 cannot be invoked to validate an order that is beyond the subject-matter jurisdiction of the authorityortocreateapowerofcancellationabsentfromthestatute.The present order is not being set aside merely because of a procedural defect in the appointment of its signatory; its fundamental infirmity is that t2 Section 68(2) does not authorize cancellation of a registered instrument on the grounds relied upon by the respondents.

27. The impugned action is also deficient on the touchstone of natural justice. The petitioner was not afforded an effective opportunity of hearing before cancellation of an instrument under which she claims proprietary rights. Articles 23 and 24 of tlrle constitution protect property rights, while Article 10-A guarantees due process in the determination of civil rights and obligations. An administrative action carrying serious civil consequences must conform to the principle of. audi alteram partern. The absence of an effective hearing provides an additional ground for interference. Article 35 of the constitution and Article 5 of the Qanun-e- Shahadat order, 1984, referred to in connection with the transaction between husband and wife, do not require a conclusive determination in these proceedings, as the genuineness and validity of the instrument remain matters for the competent civil court.

28. The objections concerning the use of stamp paper issued in 2018 for an instrument registered on 30.03.2023, tJre computerization of revenue records under the e-Pardat system and the role of the concerned Patwari under the relevant notification do not confer any additional power of cancellation upon the Registrar. These matters may be examined by the competent forum, where relevant, in accordance with law' The computerization of revenue records is an administrative measure and cannot create jurisdiction to adjudicate title or cancel a registered instrument. Any issue concerning stamp duty or the proper use of stamp paper must likewise be considered under the applicable law by the competent authoritY or court.

29.Thefourfact-findinginquiriesandletterdatedl5.l0'2o25are preliminary administrative proceedings and inter-departmental communications. Their findings may be considered for lawful departmental purposes' including examination of any misconduct by public officiats. However, such frndings do not constitute a judicial determination of proprietary rights and cannot be treated as a decree cancelling a registered instrument' The authorities concerned may proceed in accordance with law regarding any alleged official misconduct' but cannot use the inquiries as a substitute for proceedings before a competent civil court.

30. It is also pertinent that the official respondents instituted a separate constitutional petition challenging the same impugned order and inquiry proceedings. The said petition has been dismissed by this court through a sepafate order of even date on the ground of lack of jurisdiction. The present petition, however, is being decided independently on its own record and in the light of the reliefs sought herein' 3l . In view of the foregoing discussion, we hold that the powers conferred upon the Registrar under section 68(2) of the Registration Act, 1908, are supervisory and corrective in nature and do not extend to cancellation of an instrument after its registration has been completed on allegations of fraud, impersonation, misrepresentation or want of title' Such disputes require adjudication by a competent civil court' The impugned order was passed beyond the jurisdiction conferred by the Act and without affording the petitioner an effective opportunity of hearing' It is, therefore, unsustainable in law.

33. It is clarifred that this judgment shall not be construed as a declaration of title in favour of the petitioner or as a conclusive determination of the genuineness, validity or legal effect of the transaction. The interference made herein is confined to the lack of jurisdiction of the authority to cancel the registered instrument through the impugned administrative order. Any competent civil court seized of the matter shall decide the controversy independently, on the basis of the pleadings and evidence produced before it, without being influenced by observations which are confined to the jurisdictional issue decided herein.
